breakdown.fullRead:
Why does asking someone you love to change so often leave you both cross, with the job undone? You remind them, then remind them again, and maybe add a sigh. The reminders get sharper. The other person gets quieter, or snaps back. A small chore ends up standing between two people who care about each other, and it still isn't done.

The trouble, says Stanford behavior scientist BJ Fogg, is the tool you grab. Reminders, nagging and guilt all try to make someone want it more. But wanting is the least steady part of any habit. It rises and falls with the day, the mood and the workload. Pushing on it rarely moves it far, and it often makes people dig in. Guilt is no better, since people change best when they feel good, not bad.

His answer is to help others the way you help yourself. The same steps work on another person's habits as on your own, and their drive is the last thing to touch. He holds to two rules here. Help people do what they already want to do. Help them feel successful. In practice, that means asking what makes the task hard for them, then making that part easier, with each step small enough to feel like a win.

Think of a wet towel left on the bedroom floor every morning. The usual move is to point at it again. The other move is to ask, calmly, what makes hanging it up a pain. The answer might be that the only hook is behind the bathroom door, already full of robes. A second hook beside the shower fixes that in five minutes. Nobody had to care more. The task just got easier.

Mike, a father, learned this at home. His grown son Chris lived with him, and Mike wanted him to clean the coffee maker's filter. Pushing only made Chris resent it, and the filter stayed dirty. So Mike stopped asking for the whole chore. He asked his son just to take the filter out, and thanked him. Then he asked him to rinse it, then to put it back, and thanked him for each step. Chris ended up cleaning the filter without being asked.

Each part of that worked for a reason. No single request was big enough to fight about, so there was nothing to push back against. Each thank-you turned a chore into a small success, and a success is something people like to repeat. Mike stopped leaning on his son's drive and changed the size of the job instead. Fogg suggests sharing a small celebration with the other person too, so the good feeling belongs to both of you.

You can do this in the open or quietly. Fogg calls the open way being a Ringleader: you lead a person, a family or a team through these steps, with their say in each one. The quiet way he calls being a Ninja: you make a helpful change without announcing it, like adding that second hook. Either way, he keeps it to changes the other person already wants. It works at home, at work and on teams.

Nagging feels like doing something. Yet each reminder turns a chore into a fight and breeds resentment, as it did with Chris. An easy step with a thank-you has no loser, so it can happen again. Pushing leaves you both cross because it leans on wanting, which never holds still. When someone you love won't change, find the part that's hard for them and shrink it.

examples.title: Dried clay on a shared pottery wheel
examples.scenario: Farah and her husband Dmitri share a pottery wheel in their garden shed. After every session he leaves wet clay splashed across the wheel, and by Saturday it has dried hard. She has reminded him four times this month. Now she hears him rinsing his hands at the shed tap, and another reminder is already on her tongue.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the reminder. Ask Dmitri what makes cleaning the wheel a pain, then fix that part, like keeping a sponge and bucket beside it.
examples.whyItMatters: A fifth reminder makes cleanup a fight he has to lose; an easier cleanup is one he can simply do.

examples.title: The blank lines in the color book
examples.scenario: Delphine trains apprentices at her hair salon. Her newest, Tomás, never writes the color mix in the client book after an appointment. She reminded him daily, then sighed about it loudly in front of a client. Now he goes quiet whenever she walks past, and the book still has blank lines where last week's mixes belong.
examples.whatToDo: Ask Tomás privately what makes the book hard to fill in, then cut it to one line before each client leaves.
examples.whyItMatters: The sighing turned the book into a test he kept failing; one easy line feels like a win he can repeat.

examples.title: Nap times nobody has a minute to write
examples.scenario: Anneliese leads the toddler room at a busy nursery. She needs her coworker Jabari to note when each child falls asleep, because parents ask at pickup. Nap time means twelve toddlers settling at once, and he never has a spare minute. When she brings it up, he says, "I'll do it when there's a second. There never is."
examples.whatToDo: Ask him what eats his time at nap, then shrink the task: a chart and pen hung by the cots, one time per child.
examples.whyItMatters: With no spare minute, only a step that takes seconds will happen, and asking him shows where those seconds are.

questions.prompt: Your teenage son leaves his bike lying across the driveway. For two weeks you remind him each evening and tell him you nearly drove over it. What most likely happens next?
choices: He starts parking it properly, since the daily reminders have finally sunk in.
He grows short with you, and the bike keeps ending up in the driveway.
He starts leaving it by the garage, now that he understands how close it came.
questions.explanation: Two weeks of pushing turns the bike into a fight, so moving it starts to feel like giving in. Knowing about the near miss doesn't make parking it any easier.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you, "My dad won't use the blood pressure cuff his doctor gave him. I'm going to call him every morning until he does." What's your best reply?
choices: "Ask him what makes the cuff a hassle, and fix that part first."
"Try to make him see how serious his blood pressure really is."
"That might work, but it would land better if his doctor called him instead."
questions.explanation: Asking finds what makes the cuff a hassle, so that part can be made easier. A call from the doctor is still pressure, and it does nothing about the hassle itself.

questions.prompt: Your roommate never took out the recycling. You asked what made it hard, and she said the bin sat in a cupboard behind the mop. You moved it beside the back door, and now she takes it out. Why did this work?
choices: Asking showed you cared, so she wanted to help you more.
She felt guilty once she saw you had gone to all that trouble.
You took away the hard part, so taking it out became easy.
questions.explanation: Digging the bin out from behind the mop was the hard part. With it by the back door, the chore takes almost no effort. Guilt would have pushed on her feelings and left the bin where it was.

questions.prompt: Your mother walks less each year, and you'd love her to move more. You've bought her good shoes and sent her articles about walking. What's your first move now?
choices: Ask what gets in the way, and offer one short walk to the corner.
Book her a weekly walking group, so she has people expecting her there.
Plan a long walk for the two of you this Saturday, to get her excited.
questions.explanation: Asking finds what stops her, and a walk to the corner is easy enough to happen. A long Saturday walk leans on excitement, which fades, and makes walking feel bigger, not easier.

questions.prompt: A team lead wants a coworker to keep the shared task board up to date. At every morning meeting she reminds him, adding that everyone else manages it. Where is the trap?
choices: Raising it in the meeting, when a quiet word would sting less.
Comparing him to others instead of asking what makes the board a chore.
Treating it as a favor, when it should be part of his job review.
questions.explanation: Saying everyone else manages it is pressure: it pushes on how he feels and ignores what makes the board hard. A quiet word would just be the same push, said more softly.

questions.prompt: Your partner dreads folding laundry. Instead of asking for the whole basket, you ask them to fold just the towels, and you thank them each time. What's likely after a few weeks?
choices: They fold towels only as long as you keep thanking them.
They resent being handed the smallest job, and the towels just pile up.
They start folding the towels themselves, often before you think to ask.
questions.explanation: A small job with a thank-you feels like a success, not a fight, so it keeps happening until it's theirs. Being handed the easy part gives them nothing to resent.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "My sister keeps missing our Sunday video call. I'm about to tell her how much it hurts Mum." What would you say back?
choices: "Tell her straight that if she skips again, you'll stop calling."
"Ask her what makes Sundays hard, and move the call if needed."
"Let it go for now; she'll come round once she starts missing you."
questions.explanation: Asking what makes Sundays hard finds the real snag, and moving the call makes joining easy. Waiting for her to miss you leans on wanting, which comes and goes.

reviewCards.front: Before you remind someone close to you about a chore for the fifth time, first ask them ...
reviewCards.back: ... what makes it hard for them. Then make that part easier, small enough that they can do it without a fight.

reviewCards.front: Every Sunday a man showed his wife how much money they were wasting, hoping she'd start using their budget app. Now she won't open it. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He used guilt, which pushes on how she feels and turns the app into a fight. Asking what made the app a pain would have shown him what to fix.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what do you do when someone you love keeps not changing a habit?
reviewCards.back: Stop pushing. Ask what makes it hard for them, make that part easier, and keep the step small enough to feel like a win.

reviewCards.front: Your partner said they'd start packing their own lunch, but most mornings they leave without one.
reviewCards.back: Ask what makes packing it hard. If mornings are the problem, shrink the job, maybe to setting out one lunch box the night before, and thank them when they do.

reviewCards.front: Why do reminders and guilt so rarely change someone you love for good?
reviewCards.back: They try to make the person want it more, and wanting rises and falls. They also turn the task into a fight, so doing it feels like giving in.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting what blocks another person's habit and clearing it, instead of pressing them to try harder.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to a meal with someone I've been nagging, I ask what makes that task hard for them, and listen without arguing.
When I catch myself thinking someone just doesn't care enough, I shrink my request to one small step and thank them once it's done.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tonight is over, pick one thing you keep reminding someone about. Ask them, without blame, what makes it hard, and write their answer down.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each time you get home this week, notice one chore you'd usually remind someone about. Ask for just one small step of it, and thank them the moment it's done.
